title: Jetty 12: acceptors, selectors and thread pools
goal: By the end you can describe how a Jetty 12 server turns a connection into a handler call, write blocking and non-blocking core handlers, predict which thread the adaptive execution strategy uses for each, and move blocking handlers onto virtual threads.
opening:
Picture the busiest branch of our post office. At the door, a doorman lets customers in and shows each to a box. Two light-watchers each mind a section of the wall. When a light comes on, the watcher reads the label on the job. A quick job, he does on the spot. A long one, he does himself only after a standby clerk takes over the lights. With no standby free, he hands it to the pool of clerks. Doormen, watchers and clerks all come from one staff room.

That branch is Jetty 12, one of the oldest Java web servers, often embedded inside other programs. Unlike Vert.x and Quarkus, it has its own select loops on `java.nio`, not Netty's.

Its trap is the label again. Mark a slow handler "quick" because that sounds faster, and a light-watcher serves it while his section of the wall goes dark. Quarkus on Vert.x: IO threads, workers and virtual threads showed a framework that trusts labels. In this lesson, we'll count Jetty's staff, write handlers both ways, see who served each customer, and hire helpers for the slow jobs. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: A Jetty 12 server uses its default thread pool. A handler that extends `Handler.Abstract` (so it declares itself blocking) makes a 300 ms database call. Which thread usually runs it?
options: A worker thread taken from the pool's queue, the way many servers run every request
The selector thread that read the request, while a spare reserved thread takes over the selecting
A virtual thread, because Jetty 12 enables them by default
The acceptor thread that accepted the connection
warmup.why: Jetty's adaptive execution strategy prefers to run a task on the thread that produced it, while its data is still in that CPU's cache. For a blocking task it does that only when a reserved thread is free to take over selecting: the Execute-Produce-Consume mode. The demo in this lesson shows `epcRunTask` in the handler's stack. Virtual threads are off unless you configure them.

sections.h: Doormen, light-watchers and one staff room: the parts of a Jetty server
sections.body:
Jetty's documentation describes a `Server` as the component that links a collection of `Connector`s and a collection of `Handler`s, with threads from one `ThreadPool` doing all the work. A **connector** accepts connections and turns their bytes into requests. A **handler** is your code: the object that answers a request. Every thread you'll see in this lesson comes from that one pool, the staff room.

The connector you'll use is the `ServerConnector`, and it has two kinds of threads. **Acceptors**, one by default, call `accept()` and hand each new connection on: they're the doormen. A `SelectorManager` owns several `ManagedSelector`s, and each `ManagedSelector` is one thread running a `java.nio` `Selector`. That's the select loop from lesson 2, which uses `epoll`, Linux's way of watching many connections at once, and each one is a light-watcher with a section of the wall.

By default there are `max(1, min(cpus / 2, maxThreads / 16))` selectors, and the docs' rule of thumb is that one selector manages 1,000 to 5,000 connections. Inside, each connection becomes an `EndPoint` that moves bytes and a `Connection` that understands a protocol, such as HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 or WebSocket.

Here is a branch with one connector and the price desk as its handler:

```java
Server server = new Server(new QueuedThreadPool());   // one pool for everything
ServerConnector connector = new ServerConnector(server);
connector.setHost("127.0.0.1");
connector.setPort(8080);
server.addConnector(connector);
server.setHandler(new PriceHandler(300));
server.start();
```

```kotlin
val server = Server(QueuedThreadPool())                // one pool for everything
val connector = ServerConnector(server).apply { host = "127.0.0.1"; port = 8080 }
server.addConnector(connector)
server.handler = PriceHandler(300)
server.start()
```

`PriceHandler` is this lesson's lab class: it answers each request after a 300 ms "database lookup". The default pool is a `QueuedThreadPool` with at least 8 and at most 200 threads. The connector leases some of them for good, which means it takes them out of the pool for as long as the server runs. `JettyThreadsDemo` starts a default server on 4 CPUs and counts:

```text
cpus=4 acceptors=1 selectors=2
QueuedThreadPool min=8 max=200 started=8 leased=3
```

One doorman and two light-watchers make three leased threads. The pool must have room for those plus at least one thread for requests. The docs suggest sizing `maxThreads` as the leased threads plus the threads you want for handlers.

Two pool rules surprise people. First, the pool's queue must be unbounded. Jetty sometimes needs to run its own tasks to make progress; HTTP/2, for example, must write in order to read. The docs warn that a rejected task can make the server grind to a halt. Limit load with a QoS handler instead, one of Jetty's handlers that caps how many requests run at once (QoS stands for quality of service). Second, a platform thread, an ordinary thread of the operating system, costs about 1 MiB of memory outside the heap, so a pool of 200 is a real amount of memory.

**One pool staffs the whole branch. Size it as leased threads plus request threads, and never bound its queue.**

The staff are in place. The next question is what your handler promises them.

sections.h: Returning true is a promise: the asynchronous core Handler API

try.title: Break the handler contract
steps: In `JettyThreadsDemo`, change the `Blocking` handler's body to just `return false;` (delete the `Content.Sink.write` line). Predict what the first GET prints.
Put it back. Now think it through without running it: what does a client see if a handler returns `true` and never completes the callback?
try.expect: With `return false` the request finds no handler, and Jetty answers with a 404 page, which the demo prints as the body. A handler that returns `true` and never completes the callback leaves the request open: the client waits until its own timeout or Jetty's idle timeout ends the connection. Returning `true` is a promise to finish the response exactly once.

sections.h: Who serves the customer: one strategy, three modes
sections.body:
When a selector finds a lit box, a readable connection, it produces a task: "run this connection's `onFillable`", which parses the request and calls your handler. Jetty's `AdaptiveExecutionStrategy` then decides which thread consumes that task. It has three main modes, named in the Jetty docs:

- Produce-Consume (PC): the selector thread runs the task itself. There's no hand-off, and the CPU's caches, its small fast memories, still hold the connection's data. But every other connection on that selector waits. The docs say this mode is equivalent to the event loop of Node.js (a JavaScript server) or Netty.
- Produce-Execute-Consume (PEC): the task goes to the thread pool. Nothing waits behind it, but there's a hand-off, a queue, and cold caches on another core.
- Execute-Produce-Consume (EPC): the selector thread runs the task, and a **reserved thread**, one the pool keeps idle and ready, takes over the selecting. Warm caches, and no stall.

In the branch, PC is the watcher serving a quick job on the spot. PEC is the watcher handing a long job to the pool. EPC is the watcher waving a standby over to the lights and serving the long job himself.

The choice follows the task's invocation type. A `NON_BLOCKING` task runs in PC mode. A `BLOCKING` task runs in EPC mode when a reserved thread is available, and in PEC mode when none is. Jetty's source notes that this strategy used to be called "Eat What You Kill": the hunter eats what it caught. `StrategyDemo` reads the mode from each handler's own stack trace, in four setups:

```text
default pool, BLOCKING       -> qtp1636182655-25 :: AdaptiveExecutionStrategy.epcRunTask
default pool, NON_BLOCKING   -> qtp2106165633-37 :: AdaptiveExecutionStrategy.pcRunTask
reservedThreads=0, BLOCKING  -> qtp1090541608-50 :: no strategy frame: dispatched to the pool
virtual threads, BLOCKING    -> jetty-vt-1 :: VirtualThread.run
```

`qtp` threads belong to the `QueuedThreadPool`. The blocking handler ran in EPC mode, and the non-blocking one in PC mode. With no reserved threads, nobody could take over the lights, so the blocking task went to the pool, and its stack has no strategy frame at all. The fourth line waits for the next section.

Now you can see why the handler's declaration matters. `NonBlocking` is a promise that lets Jetty run your code on the selector thread, exactly like a Netty event loop. Break the promise with a database call, and every connection on that selector stalls; the docs call it a risk of server lock-up. In the branch, the watcher is busy with a long job, and his whole section of the wall goes unwatched.

Containers, handlers that hold other handlers, combine their children's types. So one blocking handler anywhere in a handler tree makes the whole tree blocking, which is safe, but it costs the PC fast path.

Compare that with the other servers you know. Netty-based servers, including Vert.x and Quarkus, run every handler in PC mode on the event loop, and moving work off it is your job. Tomcat, another widely used Java web server, watches connections with a poller thread and runs each request on its executor's threads, 200 by default. Jetty sits in between: it chooses per task, from what your handler declares.

**A handler's superclass decides which thread runs it. Declare `NonBlocking` only for code that never waits.**

The fourth line of the demo ran on a virtual thread. Jetty 12 offers two ways to get there.

try.expect: Blocking on the default pool: `epcRunTask`. Non-blocking: `pcRunTask`, on the selector's own thread. With no reserved threads, a blocking task can't use EPC, because nobody could take over selecting, so it is dispatched to the pool and the handler's stack has no strategy frame at all (PEC). sections.h: Temporary helpers again: virtual threads in Jetty 12
sections.body:
A **virtual thread** is a cheap thread that the JDK parks while it waits, on top of a few **carrier** threads from the operating system. In the branch, it's a temporary helper hired for one job. Jetty 12 offers virtual threads in two ways, and they behave very differently.

The first way keeps the `QueuedThreadPool` and gives it a virtual threads executor:

```java
QueuedThreadPool pool = new QueuedThreadPool(12);
pool.setVirtualThreadsExecutor(VirtualThreads.getNamedVirtualThreadsExecutor("price-vt-"));
```

```kotlin
val pool = QueuedThreadPool(12)
pool.virtualThreadsExecutor = VirtualThreads.getNamedVirtualThreadsExecutor("price-vt-")
```

When the strategy picks PEC for a blocking task, it now sends the task to a virtual thread instead of a pool thread. Turning this on sets the reserved threads to zero by default, so blocking tasks always take that path. Acceptors, selectors and non-blocking tasks stay on platform threads. `JettyThreadsDemo` shows it: with the executor set, the blocking handler ran on `jetty-vt-0` and the non-blocking one on a `qtp` thread.

The second way is `VirtualThreadPool`, which replaces the pool. Despite its name, it doesn't pool virtual threads. It starts a new virtual thread for each task, and limits how many tasks run at once with a semaphore, a counter of permits, 200 of them by default. With it there are no `qtp` threads at all: the acceptor and the selectors run on virtual threads too.

`JettyLoadDemo` sends 40 requests at once to a handler that blocks for 300 ms, on three pools. Before you read on, predict with Little's law how many handlers each pool can run at once. One run on a busy 4-core machine printed:

```text
QueuedThreadPool(max=12)               40 x 300 ms -> 1,786 ms, at most 9 in the handler at once
QueuedThreadPool(max=12) + virtual     40 x 300 ms ->   410 ms, at most 40 in the handler at once
VirtualThreadPool(maxThreads=8)        40 x 300 ms -> 1,853 ms, at most 7 in the handler at once
```

Twelve platform threads, minus the leased ones and a reserved thread, left nine for requests, so 40 requests took five rounds of 300 ms. The virtual executor let all 40 wait at once: one round, plus the cost of starting. The `VirtualThreadPool` with 8 permits was slowest, because its permits cap concurrency below even the platform pool. Only 7 ever reached the handler at once, so at least one permit was busy with something else.

One version note from the Jetty docs. Jetty dedicates a thread to each `Selector`, and up to Java 23, calling `Selector.select()` from a virtual thread pins its carrier: the carrier can't run anyone else while the selector waits. From Java 24 it doesn't. On 21 to 23, then, a server that runs everything on virtual threads loses one carrier per selector.

That's one more reason to prefer the first way. `QueuedThreadPool` plus the virtual threads executor keeps the light-watchers on platform threads and gives only the blocking jobs to temporary helpers. And as in every lesson of this track, helpers don't protect what's behind them: 40 handlers at once means 40 database calls at once.

**Give blocking handlers virtual threads through the `QueuedThreadPool`'s executor. Then put a real limit in front of the database.**

try.expect: About 1.7 s with at most 9 or 10 at once on the 12-thread pool (four or five rounds), about 350 to 410 ms with all 40 at once with the virtual executor, and about 1.9 to 2.1 s with at most 7 at once on `VirtualThreadPool(8)`. compare.title: The return-to-sender desk as an asynchronous Jetty handler

java.title: EchoHandler.java

kotlin.title: EchoHandler.kt

compare.note: The two are the same handler at run time. The Kotlin version shows two small differences. The `BiConsumer` passed to `whenComplete` becomes a two-parameter lambda, and `if`/`else` replaces the early `return`, because a bare `return` inside a Kotlin lambda would return from `handle` itself and doesn't compile here (you'd need `return@whenComplete`). Kotlin also lets you write Jetty's setters as properties (`server.handler = ...`, `pool.virtualThreadsExecutor = ...`). The threading is identical: the lambda runs on whichever thread completes the body future, which can be a different thread from the one that called `handle`.

worked.title: Move a blocking price service onto virtual threads

steps.say: A Jetty branch serves prices with a 300 ms database lookup per request, on a pool of 50. Under a burst of 400 requests the slowest answers take seconds. Little's law: about 45 threads can run handlers, so 400 requests need 400 / 45 x 0.3 s, about 2.7 s, to drain, while the CPU is nearly idle.
steps.alt_code:
val pool = QueuedThreadPool(50)                         // about 45 left after leasing
val server = Server(pool)
server.handler = PriceHandler(300)

steps.say: Keep the handler and give blocking tasks virtual threads. The pool keeps its platform threads for the doorman and the light-watchers; every blocking handler gets a temporary helper, so the burst no longer queues for threads.

Now the queue has moved to the database. 400 handlers all ask for one of its 20 connections. That's the right place for the wait, but give it a timeout, so a slow database turns into fast errors instead of 400 stuck requests. A database connection pool library has the same two settings, a maximum size and a connection timeout; here they are with a plain `Semaphore`.

Check that the health check is still cheap. It extends `Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking`, so it keeps running on platform threads in Produce-Consume mode, which the lab's last test asserts. If someone later adds a database ping to it, change its superclass in the same change.

lab.title: Build Jetty core handlers and give blocking ones virtual threads
steps: Run the tests. All five fail. `BranchServer` starts one branch, a Jetty server, per test; `PriceHandler` is the slow price desk, `StatusHandler` a health check, and `EchoHandler` the return-to-sender desk.

Fix `StatusHandler`'s superclass so it declares itself non-blocking. Write `PriceHandler.serve`: sleep `delayMs`, write the body from its Javadoc with `Content.Sink.write`, return `true`. The invocation-type test should pass.
Write `BranchServer.start`: `new Server(pool)`, a `ServerConnector` on host 127.0.0.1 and port 0, `setHandler`, `start()`. The platform-pool test should pass: read its assertion on `maxConcurrent()`.
Write `EchoHandler.handle` with `Content.Source.asStringAsync`, and return `true` right away.
Write `BranchServer.virtualQueuedThreadPool`. Run all five tests. The last one shows that `StatusHandler` stays on platform threads even with virtual threads enabled.
hints: `Thread.currentThread().isVirtual()` gives the `virtual=` part of the price desk's body.

If the echo test hangs and then fails, check that every path through the `whenComplete` lambda completes the callback, either with `Content.Sink.write(..., callback)` or with `Response.writeError(...)`.
With `QueuedThreadPool(12)` the connector leases one acceptor and one selector thread, and one more is kept as a reserved thread, so fewer than 12 handlers ever run at once.
If the last test fails with `virtual=true`, `StatusHandler` still extends `Handler.Abstract`, so Jetty treats it as blocking and sends it to a virtual thread.

drill.title: Write an asynchronous Jetty handler from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write a Jetty 12 core handler that reads the whole request body without blocking and answers `echo: <body>`. Which superclass, what does `handle` return, and who completes the callback?

recap: A Jetty `Server` links connectors and handlers to one `ThreadPool`. A `ServerConnector` runs acceptors (1 by default) and `ManagedSelector`s, one thread each, `max(1, min(cpus / 2, maxThreads / 16))` by default.
`QueuedThreadPool` defaults to 8 to 200 threads; connectors lease some for good, and its queue must stay unbounded. Shed load with a QoS handler.

The core API is `boolean handle(Request, Response, Callback)`: return `true` and complete the callback exactly once, maybe later. Read bodies as `Content.Source` chunks and release them, or use helpers like `asStringAsync`.
`AdaptiveExecutionStrategy` runs `NON_BLOCKING` tasks on the selector thread (PC), runs `BLOCKING` ones on the selector thread while a reserved thread takes over (EPC), or hands them off (PEC).

`setVirtualThreadsExecutor` sends only blocking tasks to virtual threads; `VirtualThreadPool` runs everything virtually and caps tasks with a semaphore. Before Java 24, selectors on virtual threads pin carriers.
The limit: Jetty trusts the declaration. A `NonBlocking` handler that waits stalls its whole selector, and virtual threads still limit nothing behind the handler.
closing:
We started in a busy branch with a doorman, two light-watchers and one staff room. Jetty 12 names them acceptors, managed selectors and a `QueuedThreadPool`, and its adaptive strategy reads each handler's label to decide who serves the customer.

Now search your own Jetty handlers for `Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking`, and check that none of them waits on a database, a lock or a slow web service.

Next, we'll go under all these servers, down to the kernel. How does a file travel to a socket without passing through your program, and what are epoll and io_uring really doing?

quiz.q: A Jetty 12 handler extends `Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking` and calls a slow web service that takes 200 ms, the blocking way. What happens under load?
options: Nothing special: Jetty moves it to a worker because the call blocks
It runs on a selector thread in Produce-Consume mode, so other connections on that selector wait behind each call
Jetty throws an exception because non-blocking handlers can't block
It runs on a virtual thread, so blocking is free
quiz.why: `NonBlocking` is a declaration Jetty trusts. It runs the task on the selector thread with no hand-off, like a Netty event loop. Jetty can't see that the call blocks, and only blocking tasks ever go to virtual threads.

quiz.q: A team gives Jetty's `QueuedThreadPool` a bounded queue of 1,000 tasks, so that it rejects work under overload. What do the Jetty docs say?
options: Good practice: a bounded queue protects the heap
Fine, as long as the bound is above maxThreads
The queue must be unbounded: Jetty needs its own tasks to run to make progress, and rejecting one can stall the server; use a QoS handler instead
Only HTTP/1.1 connectors support bounded queues
quiz.why: Jetty submits its own tasks to the same pool; for example, HTTP/2 must be able to write in order to read. A rejected internal task can stall connections. Limit load with a QoS handler, which works at the level of requests.

quiz.q: On a 4-CPU machine, `new Server(new QueuedThreadPool(64))` with one default `ServerConnector`. How many selector threads?
quiz.why: `max(1, min(cpus / 2, maxThreads / 16))` = `max(1, min(2, 4))` = 2. The selector count follows CPUs and pool size, not the number of connections.

quiz.q: From lesson 2: a Jetty `ManagedSelector` wraps a `java.nio.channels.Selector`. Why does it run on its own dedicated thread?
options: A selector's selected-key set isn't safe for use by several threads, so one thread owns each selector and its loop
`Selector.select()` must run on the main thread
Selectors are faster on platform threads
The JDK allows only one selector per thread
quiz.why: The `Selector` Javadoc says the selector itself is thread-safe but its key sets are not. One owner thread per selector is the pattern every framework uses: Netty's event loop, Vert.x's event loop, Jetty's `ManagedSelector`.

quiz.q: You enable `QueuedThreadPool.setVirtualThreadsExecutor(...)` on JDK 21. Which of these runs on a virtual thread?
options: The acceptor
The `ManagedSelector` loops
A `Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking` health check
A `Handler.Abstract` handler that calls a database
quiz.why: Only tasks the strategy runs in PEC mode, which are blocking tasks, go to the virtual threads executor. Acceptors, selectors and non-blocking handlers stay on platform threads, which also keeps selectors from pinning carriers before Java 24.

flashcards.front: What does a Jetty 12 `ServerConnector` run on threads?
flashcards.back: Acceptors (1 by default) that accept connections, and `ManagedSelector`s, one thread each, each running a `java.nio` select loop.

flashcards.front: Default number of selectors in a Jetty 12 `ServerConnector`?
flashcards.back: `max(1, min(cpus / 2, maxThreads / 16))`: 2 on 4 CPUs with the default 200-thread pool.
`boolean handle(Request, Response, Callback)`: return `true` if you take the request, then complete the callback exactly once, possibly after `handle` returns. `false` means "not mine".

flashcards.front: PC, EPC, PEC in one line each?
flashcards.back: PC: the selector thread runs the task. EPC: the selector thread runs it while a reserved thread takes over selecting. PEC: the task is handed to the pool (or a virtual thread).

flashcards.front: When does Jetty run a task in Produce-Consume mode?
flashcards.back: When the task is `NON_BLOCKING`, for example a handler that extends `Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking`.
The first sends only blocking tasks to virtual threads and keeps selectors on platform threads. The second runs everything on new virtual threads with a semaphore cap (200 by default).

flashcards.front: Why must Jetty's thread pool queue be unbounded?
flashcards.back: Jetty submits its own tasks to the pool to make progress (HTTP/2 must write to read); rejecting one can stall the server. Use a QoS handler to limit load.

terms.plain: The Jetty component that accepts connections and turns their bytes into requests.
A thread that calls `accept()` and hands each new connection to a selector.
Jetty's wrapper around one `java.nio` `Selector`, run by one thread.
A pool thread that a connector takes for good, for an acceptor or a selector.
A task's or handler's declaration: `BLOCKING`, `NON_BLOCKING` or `EITHER`.
An idle pool thread kept ready, so a selector thread can hand off selecting and run a task itself.
Jetty's per-task choice between running a task in place and handing it off (once called Eat What You Kill).
The object a Jetty handler completes, by success or failure, when its response is done.

explain_back.prompt: A colleague says "Jetty is just a server that runs every request on a thread from its pool". Explain what Jetty 12 actually does between reading a connection and calling a handler, and why a handler's superclass matters.
explain_back.answer: A Jetty connector has an acceptor thread that accepts connections, the doorman, and selector threads that each run a java.nio select loop, the light-watchers. When a selector sees a readable connection, it produces a task that parses the request and calls the handler, and the adaptive execution strategy decides who runs that task. If the handler declares itself non-blocking (`Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking`), the selector thread runs it directly, like an event loop, with no hand-off. If it declares itself blocking (`Handler.Abstract`), the selector thread still runs it when a reserved thread is free to take over selecting, which keeps caches warm; otherwise the task goes to the thread pool, or to a virtual thread if that executor is configured. So Jetty is neither purely a thread per request nor purely an event loop: it chooses per task, from the declaration. That's why the superclass matters. A handler that claims to be non-blocking and then calls a database stalls every connection on its selector, while an honest blocking declaration costs at most a hand-off to another thread.

deeper.body:
Three details from the Jetty 12.1 sources and docs round out the picture.

There is a fourth mode. `AdaptiveExecutionStrategy`'s Javadoc names Produce-Invoke-Consume for tasks whose invocation type is `EITHER`: they are run with `Invocable.invokeNonBlocking`, which asks the task to proceed in a non-blocking way if it can. The selection order is PC for a non-blocking task, EPC if a reserved thread is available, PIC for `EITHER`, and PEC otherwise. Strategies also nest: the selector's strategy produces connection tasks, and an HTTP/2 connection runs its own strategy over its streams.

Jetty also has the mirror image of a declared handler. `Request.demand(Runnable)`, which asks Jetty to call you back when more body content is available, treats a plain lambda as blocking. If your callback really is non-blocking, pass an `Invocable.Task` that says so, or Jetty may hand it to another thread for nothing.

On sizing: each connector leases a thread per acceptor and per selector, and `ReservedThreadExecutor` leases its reserved threads, by default `max(1, ceilToNextPowerOfTwo(min(cpus, maxThreads / 8)))`, or 0 once a virtual threads executor is set. The docs suggest `maxThreads` = leased threads + threads you want for handlers, and remind you that idle threads shrink back according to `idleTimeout`. Raising `maxThreads` into the thousands is the old fix for blocking handlers; on JDK 21 or newer, the virtual threads executor is the cheaper one.

HTTP/3 shows how far the connector idea stretches. Jetty implements HTTP/3 in Java but uses the native Quiche library for QUIC, the network protocol under HTTP/3, through JNA, with a connector that has zero acceptors and a single selector over a `DatagramChannel`.
